title: Leakage, the bug that makes you look brilliant
story:
The defining property of this bug is that it announces itself as success. Every other failure in this track shows up as an error, a wrong number or a model that will not train. This one shows up as a score better than anyone dared hope for, arriving at the exact moment you would most like to stop checking.

The formal definition is worth having precisely: the introduction of information about the target that should not be legitimately available to mine from. Kaufman, Rosset, Perlich and Stitelman, who set it out, list it among the top ten mistakes in the field and make a point that beginners consistently miss — the illegitimate information is almost never put there deliberately. It is facilitated by the data collection, aggregation and preparation process. Nobody adds the answer as a column. The answer arrives through how the rows were gathered and joined.

Their example is the one to memorise, because it defeats every intuition about what a suspicious column looks like. In the 2008 KDD Cup, on detecting breast cancer from mammography, the Patient ID field — dismissed as irrelevant by most competitors, because what could an identifier possibly know — turned out to have tremendous and unexpected predictive power. The identifiers traced the medical sources that had been joined together to assemble the data, and some of those sources, clinical studies among them, contributed mostly patients who have cancer. The identifier predicted the diagnosis while carrying no medical meaning whatsoever. No amount of thinking about mammography would have found it. It was a fact about the assembly of the file.

If that sounds like a competition curiosity, it is not. A survey of fields that have adopted these methods found leakage in 17 of them, affecting 294 papers, in some cases producing wildly overoptimistic conclusions — with a taxonomy of eight distinct types, running from textbook errors all the way to open research problems. The last category is worth sitting with: not every kind of leakage is a mistake somebody made, and some of them nobody currently knows how to rule out.

The cheapest demonstration is on pure noise, and you can run it in a minute. Take 200 samples, 10,000 random features and random labels, so the true accuracy is chance. Select the best 25 features using all the data, then split, and the test accuracy comes out at 0.76. Split first and fit the selector on the training portion alone, and it comes out at 0.5, which is the truth. Nothing in that experiment contains signal. The 0.76 was manufactured entirely by letting one preprocessing step see the rows it would later be judged on — and the same documentation notes that this risk attaches to almost every transformation, not just feature selection.

problem.name: Data leakage
problem.shape: A model is evaluated on data it has not seen, and information about the answer has reached that data by a route nobody designed.
tell: the score is far better than the field achieves on comparable problems
a feature near the top of the importance ranking has no business being there
an identifier, a row order or a file of origin carries predictive power
a preprocessing step was fitted before the data was split
problem.move: Ask of every feature whether it would have been available at the moment of prediction, which is a different question from whether it is in the dataset. Fit every step that learns from data inside the training portion only. Then shuffle the labels and run the whole pipeline again — a correct one scores at chance, and anything above chance is the size of the leak.
problem.invariant: The model may only use information that existed and was knowable at prediction time. Everything else inflates the estimate rather than the ability, and the inflation appears in the score rather than in an error.
problem.breaks: Feature-by-feature inspection assumes the leak has a meaning you can recognise. The hardest cases carry no meaning at all — an identifier that encodes which source a row was joined from leaks because of how the file was assembled, so no reasoning about the subject matter will reach it, and only knowledge of the data's provenance or the shuffled-label test will.

cost.time: one extra run of the pipeline on shuffled labels, plus a provenance question per field, against a failure whose symptom is indistinguishable from success
cost.beats: inspecting features for plausibility, which finds the leaks that look like leaks and misses the ones that look like nothing

worked.problem: Your model scores far better than anyone expected. What do you do?
worked.reasoning:
Treat it as a leakage hypothesis, not as a result, and go looking before anyone else does.

The reasoning is about base rates. Problems that matter are usually hard, and a score far above what the field achieves on similar problems is evidence about your pipeline before it is evidence about your model. The asymmetry is brutal: if you are right, a day of checking costs a day. If you are wrong and you ship, the correction happens in production, in front of the people you showed the number to.

First check what the model is actually using. Rank the features by importance, and look hard at anything near the top that should not be near the top. Two patterns account for most of it. Something recorded after the outcome — a field that only gets populated once the thing you are predicting has already happened, a date, a status, a flag set downstream. And something that encodes how the data was assembled rather than what it describes, which is the KDD Cup case: an identifier with tremendous predictive power because the identifiers traced the sources that were joined, and the sources had different rates of the outcome. That second kind is the one to fear, because no amount of domain reasoning about the subject matter will surface it. It is a fact about the file, not about the world.

Second, check the boundary. Was every step that learns from data fitted inside the training portion, or did something see everything first? The documentation's rule is blunt — never call fit on the test data — and the usual violation is a preprocessing step that ran before the split. That includes scaling, imputation, feature selection, dimensionality reduction and any encoding computed from the target.

Third, run the noise test, because it is decisive and it takes a minute. Shuffle the labels and run the entire pipeline again, end to end. With the relationship destroyed, a correct pipeline must score at chance. If it still beats chance, the score is measuring a route from the answer into the features, and you have found the leak without having to guess which column carries it.

The framing I would offer is the separation the original authors proposed: everything the model sees must be information that would have been available at the moment the prediction is made. Not available in the dataset — available at prediction time. Those two are different, and the gap between them is where this lives.

problem.practice: Take your best-scoring model and run it once on shuffled labels, end to end, including every preprocessing step. Write down what it scores. Then take its top five features and answer, for each, whether that value existed at the moment the prediction would be made — not whether it is in the table.

beats.broke: A model is scored by showing it data it has not seen, and information about the answer reaches that data through routes nobody designed — how the rows were gathered, joined, ordered and prepared.
beats.fix: Separate what is known at prediction time from what is known afterwards, and enforce that separation structurally rather than by inspection, because the leaking column often has no semantic relationship to the target at all.
beats.cost: The separation has to be decided per field from knowledge of how the data was produced, which is information outside the dataset — and the symptom of getting it wrong is a good score rather than a bad one.

interview.q: Your model scores far better than anyone expected. What do you do?
interview.trap: Accepting it, or looking only for features that seem semantically suspicious. The canonical case was a patient identifier with no medical meaning, which predicted cancer because the identifiers traced which sources had been joined to build the file.
interview.answer:
Treat it as a leakage hypothesis rather than a result, and go looking before anyone else does.

The reasoning is about base rates. Problems worth solving are usually hard, so a score far above what the field achieves on comparable problems is evidence about the pipeline before it is evidence about the model. And the asymmetry is unforgiving: a day of checking costs a day, while shipping a leaked model means the correction happens in production, in front of the people you showed the number to.

I would check three things. First, what the model is actually using — rank the features and look at anything near the top that has no business being there. Two patterns cover most cases: a field recorded only after the outcome occurred, and a field that encodes how the data was assembled rather than what it describes. The second is the dangerous one. In the 2008 KDD Cup on detecting cancer from mammography, the patient identifier had tremendous and unexpected predictive power because the identifiers traced the medical sources that had been joined together, and some of those sources contributed mostly patients who had cancer. No amount of domain reasoning about mammography surfaces that; it is a fact about the file.

Third, the noise test, which is decisive and takes a minute. Shuffle the labels and re-run the entire pipeline. With the relationship destroyed, a correct pipeline scores at chance; if it still beats chance, the score is measuring a route from the answer into the features, and I have found the leak without having to guess which column carries it.

The framing I would keep is the separation the original authors proposed: the model may only see information that would have been available at the moment of prediction. Available in the dataset and available at prediction time are different things, and the distance between them is exactly where this bug lives.

takeaway: Leakage is the only bug in this track whose symptom is a better score, it usually arrives through how the data was assembled rather than through any meaningful column, and one run on shuffled labels will measure it without your having to guess where it came from.
